# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's

post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):

- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

insights_note: no grouping to read (no follow-up line with two answers)

founder.order_why: The look-back window (screen 4) sits between two screens that both carry the same 'define exactly where this idea applies' question (3 and 5), so the context step is split in an odd place; the problem and sending steps that follow run in a sensible order.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.', with the window question between them; it reads as the context being asked for twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asked about over-requesting itself. Both belief questions (8 and 9) count only jobs that failed mid-run, but my problem has two sides: under-request and the job dies, over-request and the cluster wastes 30% to 59% of its GPU hours. 'Everyone over-requests by two to three times' is the common case and the waste I actually charge for, so I expected a belief question like 'how many out of 10 padded a request beyond what the job used'. Frequency also counts days, but my researchers submit several jobs a working day, so I'd want to say how many submissions are mis-sized, not just how many days had a failure.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks what I'd most like made easier before screen 5 asks how guessing memory, time and GPUs went, so I'm picking a pain point before being walked back to the guessing that caused my mid-run failure; the two would read better swapped.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the job failed mid-run (out of memory or hitting the time limit from under-requesting, versus a node or code fault), how much work or how many days were lost when it died, and whether I now over-request to be safe and wait longer in the queue because of it.

screens.why1: Right after I typed how researchers size jobs today, checking the five rungs of how that went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Four rungs read like my researchers talk, but 'The job ran, but I had asked' is cut off mid-thought and I have to guess it means they asked for far more than the job used.
screens.why3: Any researcher on a SLURM or K8s cluster knows whether their last job ran first time, got resubmitted or died at walltime.
screens.why4: The usual case, a job that ran but held two to three times what it used, appears only as the garbled 'The job ran, but I had asked', so most researchers' true answer is unreadable; the other rungs only grade failures.
screens.why5: My problem is waste as much as failure, and the scale has drifted to failures only, with the over-request rung truncated and the belief opening on 'their way of guessing' instead of the bare act.
screens.why7: Five rungs run best to worst with a working first rung and outright failure last, but rung 2 is broken text and the stated bar also names 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle', which is not on the final list; the padded run sits above the line as if it did the job, which bends the one-measure and line rules.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did sizing it go? The job ran first time, sized about right / It ran, but I padded it about 2x / It ran, but held 3x or more than it used / It failed partway and I resubmitted / It never ran to the end, then I can't recall (line under rung 1)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out to researchers, after the problem steps are set.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a preview each and a flat 400-credit cost are plain on first read, though the hint packs four facts into one paragraph.
screens.why3: Picking the voice that will speak to my own researchers is my call and needs nothing I don't know.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a five-second preview, and a preselected default covers the 'I don't mind' case without a separate escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing of my problem, product or roles is rewritten here; it only picks a voice for the questions I already checked.
screens.instead: Who should ask them your questions? (Daphne is picked; tap ▶ to hear Daphne or Saskia — 400 credits either way, sent by text message.)

screens.why1: Choosing how researchers will answer belongs right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, so its place is obvious.
screens.why2: AI interviewer on video, read and tap, or let them choose are plain to me, and the descriptions say what each one does in a sentence.
screens.why3: I know my researchers sit at a terminal and would rather read and tap between jobs than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete: voice, text, or both offered with the researcher picking, and no escape is needed for a choice the founder makes.
screens.why5: It names my segment as I typed it and leaks nothing of the product to the respondent.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how researchers answer, the obvious next thing is who gets the link, so this closes the send step naturally.
screens.why2: Each choice is plain on first read; 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own page, and its gloss says what it is.
screens.why3: I know who I'm reaching, the researchers I know on HPC and GPU clusters, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search list, or one open link posted where researchers gather (a cluster Slack or mailing list) cover my real ways in, and none overlap; the second option's slip from 'I' to 'you' is cosmetic.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name, each with their own link, is kept as I gave it, and nothing of Expanse leaks into the options.
screens.instead: Keep it, but write the second option in the first person like the others: 'People I found with Keel -- I pick a list from the Contacts page; Keel makes a link for each, and I send them.'

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' has '4 counted' beside it, but the 5 needed sits only on the cards, and it names Frequency alone when Importance and Current solution are short by the same margin.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, and the tally (1 holding, 3 too few to call, 7 answered) and Prevalence's '6 of 7 · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' read at once.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my lines word for word, but Prevalence and Frequency turn my problem into jobs failing mid-run, when my point is that everyone over-requests to avoid failure and wastes the cluster.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need one more counted answer per card, but nothing says why three people went uncounted or what to do next for the idea.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, the low counts are called too few rather than read as signal, and Prevalence holding is marked as exactly at the bar rather than strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: three of four beliefs have 4 of the 5 counted answers needed (3 of 7 people weren't counted), so get a few more researchers through before reading Frequency, Importance or Current solution; failure mid-run is at the bar at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against over 7 people on a 0-to-7 axis, with my bar marked at 6 and labelled 'at least 8 in 10', so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The failed-mid-run job and my 'at least 8 in 10' are mine, but the belief line and 'Common among these 7' drop my segment's qualifier ('on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs'), and the Asked line's '— the most recent time it happened' tag doesn't fit a yes/no gate a No answers too.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me it is common at exactly my bar and points me to the next two cards, but it doesn't say what that means for Expanse, for example that a single further No would have dropped it below the bar.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and 'at your bar exactly' keeps 'Holding up' from reading as strong.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 researchers and ML engineers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100+ GPUs had a job fail mid-run in the last 5 working days: 6 of 7 said yes, exactly your bar, so one more No would have sunk it; treat it as a lean and widen the sample before leaning your pitch on failures.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The median at 4 and the strip are plain, but the chart's 0 tick is a step nobody could pick, and 'your bar · 4 of 5' next to 4 cells all for me takes a second look before I see it means four of the five needed, not a bar already met.
screens.why_b3: My problem is guessing memory, GPUs and walltime at every submission, padding two to three times so jobs don't die; 'have a cluster job fail mid-run on 3 to 5 working days out of 5' turns the result I say people pad to avoid into the event, which I recognise but would never claim happens most days.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that one more counted answer decides it, or that all four counted so far are at my low or above.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, why Mei-Ling and Rafael are out), the low n is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims the belief held.
screens.instead: Ask how many days I submitted a job and had to guess its memory, GPUs and run time, not how many days one failed mid-run; and say 'all 4 counted are at 3 days or more; one more counted answer at 3 or above and this holds'.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the count line and So line agree with it.
screens.why_b2: The bars are plain: 4 people, two picks each, 8 picks, and my problem leads with 3. But the bar line just repeats my item instead of stating the bar, and 'your bar · 4 of 5' with the marker at 4 takes a second look before I see it means 4 of 5 once five are counted.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, with my own 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' as the named problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of 4 already lean my way or that one more counted researcher would settle it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible at 6 answered and 4 counted, the two uncounted people are named with their reasons, and the small group is called a lean, not a call, with no overstatement.
screens.instead: 3 of 4 counted put guessing memory, GPUs and run time in their two, a lean your way; one more counted researcher settles it (4 of 5 holds), so get one more answer before reading anything into it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly above its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know it is undecided and why.
screens.why_b2: The rungs, their counts and my line under 'Padded it a little' read at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell and a marker at 4 takes a second look before I see it means 4 of the 5 needed would have to land below the line.
screens.why_b3: The title is Current solution and the belief is the line I checked word for word, with my bar named by its exact rung, 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that 3 of the 4 counted already land below my line, or that one more counted researcher landing below it would make the belief hold.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, who was left out and why), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the four counted answers carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted fell short of padding a little (two doubled everything, one died and was resubmitted), so it leans your way; one more counted researcher below the line would make it hold, so send the study to a few more people on 100+ GPU clusters.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no call yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: 'Importance' and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Expanse; it doesn't say to get one more counted researcher, or whether Kwabena's data-movement pain is worth probing, so I have to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: Every count is visible (1 against, 1 asked, 'On their own (1)'), and the single quote is not dressed up as a theme or a trend.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line is new to me: sizes taken from last week's runs are 'fine', and his day goes to moving data and getting libraries to agree, which names a competing pain I never typed.
screens.instead: Too few to call: one more counted researcher decides it; the one against already sizes from past runs and loses his day to data movement and software setup, so ask the next ones whether that outranks the guess.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it is obvious why they ask whether I'm on a big shared GPU cluster before asking anything else about my jobs.
screens.why2: "Run your jobs on a cluster" is exactly how I'd say it, and 100 GPUs is a number I can check against our cluster in my head.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our shared cluster is because I see the partition and node counts every time I submit, so I can answer this from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly for a gate, and with no escape that is right for a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of clusters with 100 or more GPUs, and nothing about a product or the founder's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and has two options, and "100 or more GPUs" says well aloud.
screens.instead: In the last week, did you submit jobs to a shared cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I run on a 100+ GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine died mid-run this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Cluster job' and 'fail mid-run' are exactly how I'd say it to my labmates, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether one of my jobs died this week because I check squeue and my logs every morning.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the recall chips belong to the story box after a Yes, so they are not the gate's escape.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed because the memory, GPUs or run time had to be guessed, but 'fail mid-run' drops that, so a crash from my own bug or a node dying would also count.
screens.why6: One short question with 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Yes and No are both possible and the gate is not the circumstance, but the condition that made it the founder's problem (the resource request running out) is dropped, so the share counts every kind of failure.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, was a job of yours killed for going over its requested memory or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to a job failing mid-run this week, asking on how many days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Cluster job" and "fail mid-run" are how I'd say it myself; I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week a run died on me, since I lose the work and have to resubmit, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5 is complete and distinct, and "I can't recall" sits apart as the only escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but "fail mid-run" covers every crash (a bug, a NaN loss, preemption, a dead node), not only a job killed because I guessed its memory or time wrong, so it drifts from the guessing problem.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, "a number from 1 to 5" is easy to hold, and the escape comes last.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of working days out of 5, from 1 to the window's count, with no 0 and no bands; the unit is said, "I can't recall" is the one escape apart, and the act happened on a given day or did not.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did a cluster job of yours get killed for hitting its memory or time limit? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often my jobs died mid-run, asking which part of running jobs I'd most like easier makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: Every row is how I'd say it myself: data on and off the cluster, getting software working, queue waits, guessing memory, GPUs and run time, and the group's allocation are all everyday SLURM talk.
screens.why3: I do every one of these myself each week, so I can pick from experience without guessing.
screens.why4: The rows are real and distinct, but 'Running out of the group's allocation' is a bad outcome rather than a task, so 'made easier' reads backwards on it, and it half-overlaps with guessing, since over-requesting is what burns the allocation.
screens.why5: The guessing row keeps the founder's three things (memory, GPUs, run time), and nothing about a product or tool reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question, then five short parallel phrases and the one escape said last, easy to hold.
screens.why7: The own row is there and not first, with four rivals, None of these at the first ask, and the belief can go either way; but one rival is an outcome rather than a task, and it partly follows from the own row, which bends the 'none a cause of another, never a bad outcome' rule.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Moving data on and off the cluster · Getting software working on the cluster · Waiting for a job to start · Guessing memory, GPUs and run time · Keeping track of the group's allocation · None of these

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how sizing my last job actually went.
screens.why2: Memory, time, GPUs, padded and resubmitted are exactly how I talk about sbatch requests, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I size every job I submit myself, so I know how the last one went: I padded the walltime and it ran with GPUs half idle.
screens.why4: 'Copied an old script and hoped' is a way of guessing, not how it went, so it overlaps every other option (my copied script ran fine, which is option one too), and the others also open with a method before the outcome.
screens.why5: It stays on guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting and leaks no product or founder terms.
screens.why6: Each option is two clauses ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), so five of them in one breath is hard to hold by ear.
screens.why7: There are working rungs above any sensible line and real shortfalls below, and the escape I can't recall fits sizing my own job, but the rungs carry methods and mix two costs (idle waste and a dead job), and the last rung is a method rather than the job failing outright.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did your memory, time and GPU request turn out? Ran fine, about what it used · Ran, some of it sat idle · Ran, much of it sat idle · Got killed, finished after resubmitting · Got killed, never finished -- or I can't recall
